This should be `char32_t`.
I'm aware other interfaces require passing `String` for padding, but that's a good excuse to fix it before this PR.

This should probably be declared on `String`.

As for the name, how about `NumberFormatOptions`?

How about this?

```suggestion
		SIGN_MINUS_ONLY, // '-'. Show sign only for negative numbers. Default.
		SIGN_PLUS_MINUS, // '+'. Always show sign.
		SIGN_SPACE_MINUS, // ' '. Show space for positive numbers, sign for negative numbers.
```

```suggestion
	bool use_base_prefix = false; // '#'
```
This should probably also be a `char32_t`, I think?

```suggestion
	uint8_t precision = 0;
```

I think using 0 to denote infinite precision is fine? Otherwise we can set it to 255 by default.

```suggestion
	enum struct Type {
		DEFAULT, // Default per argument type.
		STRING, // 's'
		CHAR, // 'c'
		DECIMAL, // 'd'
		BINARY, // 'b'
		OCTAL, // 'o'
		HEX, // 'x'
		HEX_UPPER, // 'X'
		FLOAT, // 'f'
		FLOAT_SIG_FIG, // 'h'  Float but with precision meaning significant figures.
		// TODO: Consider adding support for GENERAL, SCIENTIFIC when they have precision handling formatters in String.
		VECTOR, // 'v'
	};
	Type format_type = Type::DEFAULT;
```

+// FormatSpec specifies a configuration for string-formatting a value.
+// This can be used to directly format values with `FormatSpec::format`, or within

+// If a valid `align` value is specified, it can be preceded by a `fill` character that
+// can be any character and defaults to a space if omitted.

+// '<': Forces the field to be left-aligned within the available space (default for most values).
+// '>': Forces the field to be right-aligned within the available space (default for numbers).
+// '^': Forces the field to be centered within the available space.
+// '=': Forces the padding to be placed after the sign (if any) but before the digits.
+//
+// Note that unless a minimum field width is defined, the field width will always be
+// the same size as the data to fill it, so that the alignment option has no meaning in
+// this case.
+//
+// The `sign` option is only valid for number types and can be one of the following:
+// '+': Indicates that a sign should be used for both positive as well as negative numbers.
+// '-': Indicates that a sign should be used only for negative numbers (default).
+// ' ': Indicates that a leading space should be used on positive numbers, and a
+//      minus sign on negative numbers.
+//
+// The '#' option causes the 'alternate form' to be used for the conversion.
+// For integers in binary, octal, or hexadecimal output, this option adds the
+// respective prefix "0b", "0o", "0x", "0X" to the output value.
+//
+// When no explicit alignment is given, preceding the width field by a '0' character
+// enables sign-aware zero-padding for numbers. This is equivalent to a fill character
+// of '0' with an alignment type of '='.
+//
+// `width` is a decimal integer defining the minimum total field width, including
+// any prefixes, separators, and other formatting characters. If not specified, then
+// the field width will be determined by the content.
+//
+// The `precision` is a decimal integer indicating how many digits should be displayed
+// after the decimal point for presentation type 'f', or before and after the decimal
+// point for presentation type 'h'. For string presentation types the field indicates
+// the maximum field size - in other words, how many characters will be used from the
+// start of the field content. `precision` is not supported for integer presentation
+// types.
+//
+// The `type` determines how the data should be presented.
+//
+// The available string presentation types are:
+// 's': String format. This is the default type for strings and may be omitted.
+// None: the same as 's'.

+// The available integer presentation types are:
+// 'd': Decimal integer. Outputs the number in base 10.
+// 'b': Binary format. Outputs the number in base 2.
+// 'o': Octal format. Outputs the number in base 8.
+// 'x': Hex format. Outputs the number in base 16, using lower-case letters for
+//      digits above 9.
+// 'X': Hex format. Outputs the number in base 16, using upper-case letters for
+//      digits above 9. If '#' is specified, the prefix '0x' will be upper-cased
+//      to '0X' as well.
+// 'c': Character. Converts the integer to the corresponding unicode character
+//      before printing.
+// None: The same as 'd'.
+//
+// The available float presentation types are:
+// 'f': Fixed-point notation. For a given precision `p`, formats the number as
+//      a decimal number with at most p digits following the decimal point but
+//      with trailing 0's removed except for a zero in the tenth's digit.
+//      With no precision given, uses a precision of 6 digits.
+// 'h': Fixed-point notation but with precision specifying significant figures.
+//      For a given precision `p`, formats the number with `p` digits combined
+//      before and after the decimal point. This precision is only used to
+//      limit the number of digits following the decimal point, not to zero
+//      out any digits preceding the decimal point. For example, 1234.5678
+//      printed with a precision of 6 will print "1234.57", whereas printing
+//      12345678.9 with a precision of 6 will print "12345679".

+//
+// Vector presentation types:

+//      If `velement` is specified, it is interpreted as another format spec
+//      that will be used to format each vector element value. For example,
+//      'v[,]' applied to Vector2i(12345, 67890) will produce "(12,345, 67,890)".
+//      Options applied to the vector and options applied to its elements are
+//      independent. So for example, both the vector and its elements can have
+//      a specified width. e.g. '20v[5x]'.
+// None: The same as 'v'.
+//
+// Note that this configuration mostly follows the Python format specification
+// mini-language (https://docs.python.org/3/library/string.html#formatspec).

We have `str_compare`, doesn't it do the same?
Generally we try to avoid new non-struct enums now in the code base. How about just `ValueFormatOptions::Alignment::LEFT` etc.? Analogous to the other one :)

I think it would be wiser to structure this function like `const Error = string.append_formatted(const FormatSpec &format_spec, const Variant &p_value)`.

The reason is that returning a `String` necessitates allocation, while we actually expect multiple string and format parts to be appended after one another (probably with a reserve at the start to avoid multiple re-allocations on resize).
I did find String::chr and switched to using it because adding this String constructor seems to introduce an error on other platforms converting Variant to String.

Actually I don't know where this came from. I don't think I wrote it. Possibly a bad merge resolution. I've deleted it and nothing is complaining.

Mostly I was trying to follow the existing patterns for returning values and errors. Some issues to discuss:

* This implementation returns error messages via the return value, flagged by the r_error arg. Is your intention to use the Error enum and not error messages any more?
* I wasn't particularly careful about allocations in the implementation. Currently the final formatted string is composed piecemeal throughout the implementation as a String. So returning it directly wouldn't add any additional allocation. Would you prefer to compose this with a char32_t[] buffer?
* It seems awkward for append_formatted to be the only way to format a value. Might there be a small set of functions, one of which looks to append the formatted string while being careful with allocations?
* In general I prefer clear composable interfaces over optimizing for particular use cases, so my inclinations would be to keep FormatSpec separate. But this is not my project, so you're free to design this how you like.

> Mostly I was trying to follow the existing patterns for returning values and errors

Yes, many `String` functions return `String` instead of appending in-place. This is OK for most APIs, but I don't think it's appropriate for an API that will be used mostly in a context where multiple parts are concatenated.

> This implementation returns error messages via the return value, flagged by the r_error arg. Is your intention to use the Error enum and not error messages any more?

Yes. Usually, we use `ERR_FAIL_COND_V_MSG(condition, value, message)` for handling problematic calls.

> I wasn't particularly careful about allocations in the implementation. Currently the final formatted string is composed piecemeal throughout the implementation as a String. So returning it directly wouldn't add any additional allocation. Would you prefer to compose this with a char32_t[] buffer?

Reducing allocations is key to make this API fast (at least, it must be faster than the current `sprintf` implementation).
I would prefer to make this function act on the `char32_t[]` buffer of the `String` (`ptr()` and `length()`), like the other `append_` functions.

> It seems awkward for append_formatted to be the only way to format a value. Might there be a small set of functions, one of which looks to append the formatted string while being careful with allocations?

Most formatting functions are very direct about their inputs and outputs, such as `num_int64`. Format specs will probably only be used for interpolated strings, and possibly replace current `vformat` calls (ideally, prepared at compile time).
If a need for 'single value' formatting functions arises, we can add it then.

>  In general I prefer clear composable interfaces over optimizing for particular use cases, so my inclinations would be to keep FormatSpec separate. But this is not my project, so you're free to design this how you like.

I'd argue that `append_` is easier to compose with other variable interfaces than returning a ready string, since you aren't forcing the caller to handle a new buffer.

I see you're calling `_append_formatted_value` here. As mentioned before, I think it would be better to inline the function here instead, because this is where the format spec is found (and thus parsed).

I don't think this is an appropriate interface for this function.
By compiling a separate regex for each key, you'll parse the string quite a few times, especially if you have many keys.
Instead, it would be appropriate to loop over the string just once (manually), figure out the appropriate key on each `{` found, and if `:` is found too, parse the format spec until the next `}` is found.
It may actually result in less code than you have now, and it sure as heck will be faster :)
Since this is unchanging, this should definitely be static. Compiling the regex could be quite computationally expensive!

This is tricky. This change factors out functionality already present in String::format (you'll see it calls this four times). The purpose of this function is to add support for formatting slots regardless of whether the format arguments are Array, Dictionary, or Object. String::format is already responsible for the repeated replacement logic you're concerned about, and I haven't changed that. If I was to replace those with single passes, I'm guessing that would break many uses of String::format. 

It seems like our choices are:
- change the logic of String::format to be single-pass rather than repeated replacement, breaking uses that depend upon the repeated replacement logic
- leave String::format with this repeated replacement
- leave String::format with this repeated replacement, and add a variant function (String::format2?) that supports single-pass replacement

What do you prefer?

Oh, oof. I guess this change would require extracting some `RegExInternal` and interacting with that, to avoid `ObjectDB`.
However, it may be easy enough (and faster) to use manual parsing here anyway. I'll think about this and get back to you.

These changes are nice, but they increase your line change count. I do think they're better than the status quo, but i think it's better if you reverted the changes anyway to make your PR simpler and keep the changes focused.

Since your PR is trying to replace the existing `String::format` logic, I think the only option is option 1 and re-write it "from scratch" to be single pass. Keeping two versions of a `format` API, especially two that aren't very compatible, isn't a great idea.

This is likely to be pretty code-churny, so it may be worth it to separate out some changes into smaller steps. That is, if you're up for it. It's shaping up to be a pretty large project, at least with all my feedback 😅
I guess it's fine where it is, it can be moved when it is needed elsewhere.

Ok. I can take a pass at this in a separate PR. I do want to get confirmation from you that you're okay with this breaking existing functionality. In particular, any code that depends upon String::format using repeated replacement logic (e.g. the first replacement inserts a token that is subsequently matched and replaced by another token) will not work any more. I do think the single-pass behavior is more correct, but breaking existing code is always tricky to manage.
Done.

Also note that this PR is not intending to change any existing String::format behavior. The only thing that should change is to allow formatting of slots when they use the {xx:format} syntax, which shouldn't affect any existing usage.

> In particular, any code that depends upon String::format using repeated replacement logic (e.g. the first replacement inserts a token that is subsequently matched and replaced by another token) will not work any more.

Could you provide an example of this? And have you seen this exploited "in the wild"?

> Also note that this PR is not intending to change any existing String::format behavior. The only thing that should change is to allow formatting of slots when they use the {xx:format} syntax, which shouldn't affect any existing usage.

It makes sense to me not to change existing behavior, unless the existing behavior is inconsistent or incorrect.

e.g. placeholder "$_", template "$a and $b", values {"a":"$b", "b":"xx"}. output "$b and xx" or "xx and xx".
Clearly awkward, but it's possible that folks might use this behavior.

I have not seen it exploited 'in the wild'. But if we go ahead with this it might be worth documenting a workaround to replicate the original behavior with the corrected implementation.
